19.t: Working with data: melatonin over a day
q: Describe the normal pattern of melatonin over the day.
Low all day (5–10), rising from about 18:00, peaking at about 03:00 (85), then falling to low levels by 09:00.
Identify two differences between the two curves.
With the screen, melatonin is much lower at midnight (25 against 70), and the peak is later (about 06:00) and slightly lower.
Explain how bright screen light changes melatonin secretion.
Light, especially blue light, is detected by the retina; signals pass to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (body clock) in the hypothalamus, which inhibits melatonin release by the pineal gland.
Predict how the person would feel at 07:00 after the screen night. Explain.
Still sleepy: melatonin is still high (about 50) when they wake, because their body clock has been shifted later.
Suggest why melatonin tablets are sometimes taken for jet lag.
Taken at bedtime in the new time zone, they signal "night" and help reset the body clock.

25.t: Working with data: heart and breathing in exercise
q: Calculate the volume of air breathed per minute at rest and at 4 minutes.
Rest: 14 × 0.5 = 7 dm³ min⁻¹. At 4 min: 28 × 2.0 = 56 dm³ min⁻¹.
Compare the increase in air breathed per minute with the increase in breathing rate.
Air per minute rose 8 times, but the breathing rate only doubled: most of the increase comes from deeper breaths.
Explain how the fall in blood pH leads to faster, deeper breathing.

More CO₂ from respiration forms carbonic acid, so pH falls. Chemoreceptors (in the medulla, aorta and carotid arteries) detect this and the medulla sends more impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
Explain why the heart rate is still raised at 6 minutes.
CO₂ is still above normal (pH 7.37) and lactate must be removed and oxidised, so extra oxygen is still needed.
Suggest why an athlete’s heart rate would rise less during the same exercise.
A larger, stronger heart pumps more blood per beat, so fewer beats are needed.
